title: Cholera
render_brief: A conspicuous plain yellow cloth quarantine flag on a simple unpainted wooden pole, fixed beside a small wooden doorway fragment on a brown ground slice. Cloth has a sewn edge and hangs in shallow folds. No biohazard symbol, radiation markings, hospital cross, skull, medicine bottles, people or corpses. Bright natural yellow is essential; wood remains natural brown. This is a reconstructed warning-marker type, not a replica of a photographed house.
history:
San Diego's 1888 rules marked infected premises
with a yellow flag or a posted warning.
Cholera was among the diseases covered.

sources.title: San Diego Ordinance No. 193, approved February 20, 1888; transcription by San Diego History Center
sources.claim: Section 34 directs the health officer to mark premises with a conspicuous yellow/quarantine flag or a doorway placard following reports of smallpox, varioloid or cholera. Section 35 prohibits unauthorized removal. Supports a yellow land-based warning, not just maritime use.

uncertainties: The ordinance fixes the yellow warning function but not flag dimensions, fabric weave, pole species, mounting hardware, exact yellow dye or doorway design. These are restrained reconstruction choices.
No claim that the same sign was used at every Western trail camp or that the symbol uniquely meant cholera. No actual outbreak at a named address is depicted.
